meta.title: Europa Strata
meta.subtitle: Cultures, empires, and genetic layers from deep time to now

ancestryKeys.label: WHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Mesolithic western/central European foragers; a substrate after farming, not a living “people” label later.

ancestryKeys.label: SHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Northern foragers of Scandinavia, often modeled as WHG with extra EHG-related affinity; important Mesolithic–Neolithic north baseline before TRB and Single Grave turnovers.

ancestryKeys.label: EHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Forest-steppe/eastern foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity; key ingredient of Yamnaya with CHG-related ancestry.

ancestryKeys.label: EEF
ancestryKeys.detail: Anatolian Neolithic–related farmers who spread demically into Europe from ~6500 BC; dominant in Early Neolithic west.

ancestryKeys.label: WSH
ancestryKeys.detail: Yamnaya-related Western Steppe Herder ancestry that spreads widely after ~3000 BC via Corded Ware and kin. Often shortened WSH or “steppe.”

ancestryKeys.label: CHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Caucasus hunter-gatherer–related ancestry; often modeled inside the steppe cline rather than as a free European component.

ancestryKeys.label: Other
ancestryKeys.detail: Catch-all residual outside the main WHG–EEF–WSH (and named) components: eastern Mediterranean, East Eurasian, North African, CHG/Iran-related, Slavic/Finnic/Turkic, or poorly resolved inputs depending on period and place. Not a single deep Paleolithic cluster.

modeLegend.persistence: Substrate continues with little demographic overturn
modeLegend.replacement: Incoming ancestry largely displaces the prior gene pool
modeLegend.absorption: Incoming elite/culture absorbed into a durable local substrate
modeLegend.continuity: Deep ternary (WHG–EEF–steppe) largely stable; polity labels shift
modeLegend.cultural: Archaeological or political package spreads faster than genes

meta.linguisticDisclaimer: Languages ≠ genes. Indo-European dispersal is often correlated with steppe-related ancestry in temperate Europe, but archaeological cultures, genomes, and speech can spread independently. Confidence tags: attested (written/epigraphic), reconstructed (comparative linguistics), hypothetical (no direct evidence), mixed.
meta.mapAttribution: Base map: Natural Earth (public domain). Culture extents are schematic best-guess consensus overlays on modern borders, not precise archaeological site distributions.

glossary.name: Western Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 14,000–5,000 BC. Mesolithic foragers of western and central Europe; later a minority substrate in farmer and Bronze Age populations.

glossary.name: Eastern Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 10,000–3,500 BC. Forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity; a primary ingredient (with CHG) of Yamnaya / WSH.

glossary.name: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 9,500–4,000 BC. Northern foragers of Scandinavia—WHG-like with elevated EHG affinity—before Funnelbeaker and Single Grave turnovers.

glossary.name: Early European Farmers
glossary.text: c. 6,500–3,000 BC. Anatolian Neolithic–related farming populations (Cardial, LBK, and related) who spread into Europe with crops and herds.

glossary.name: Western Steppe Herders
glossary.text: c. 3,300–2,000 BC. Yamnaya-related steppe pastoralist ancestry that remakes temperate Europe in the third millennium BC (Corded Ware, Beaker, and related).

glossary.name: Caucasus Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 13,000–5,000 BC. Caucasus forager-related ancestry; usually modeled inside the steppe (WSH) cline rather than as a free European component.

glossary.name: Residual / unmodeled components
glossary.text: Gray “Other” in the ancestry mix is residual ancestry outside the main WHG–EEF–WSH (and named) components: eastern Mediterranean, East Eurasian, North African, CHG/Iran-related, or poorly resolved inputs depending on period and place. Not a single deep Paleolithic cluster; the side note under Ancestry mix names what that residual stands for when known.

periods.label: Forager Europe after the ice
periods.narrative: Around 8000 BC the ice has pulled back and Europe is a mosaic of forager traditions — Azilian and Tardenoisian in the west, Maglemosian wetlands in the north, Iron Gates along the Danube, Narva–Kunda toward the Baltic. Genetics split Western from Eastern Hunter-Gatherers; archaeological names are tool facies, not kingdoms. Farming, metals, and Indo-European speech all still lie ahead.
periods.culturesNote: Azilian, Sauveterrian/Tardenoisian, Maglemosian–Kongemose, Epigravettian Italy, Iron Gates, Narva/Kunda — microlithic forager facies over WHG/EHG genetics.

iberia.culture:
Society organised around mobile kinship bands rather than villages. Labour divided by age and season: coastal shellfish weeks, inland hunting stands, and curated visits to caves that still held Paleolithic images as remembered places. Personal ornaments—shell beads, ochre-stained bone—signalled affiliation more loudly than architecture. Conflict left few mass graves; violence, when present, was likely interpersonal or raid-scale.

Exchange was local-to-regional: good flint, marine shell inland, and shared projectile geometries. There were no chiefs recoverable by title; status, if ranked at all, shows in burial care and exotic beads rather than residences.

Key sites: El Mazo (Asturias shell midden sequences); Cantabrian Azilian rock shelters; Portuguese Atlantic Mesolithic middens (Tagus/Sado); Levantine Geometric Mesolithic sites.

Key people / anonymity: No historically named individuals. Social memory survives only as anonymous burial persons and site excavators’ type names.
iberia.ancestryNote: Mesolithic Iberia ≈ WHG; local structure exists but not EEF or steppe yet.
iberia.linguisticNote: No writing. Later Iberian (non-IE) and Basque are historically attested millennia later and cannot be projected onto Azilian speech.
iberia.summary: Post-glacial WHG foragers of Atlantic and Mediterranean Iberia, living by seasonal rounds of shellfish, deer, and upland game before Cardial farming.

britain.culture:
Bands managed seasonal rounds from upland hunting to estuary fishing. Timber platforms and rare ritual gear (red-deer frontlets) suggest episodic aggregation and performance beside wetlands. Ireland and Britain shared canoe-and-trap aesthetics more than carved monuments.

Social scale remained small; exotic amber or shale beads mark occasional long links without chiefdom bureaucracy.

Wetland aggregation sites hint that even low-density islands staged periodic meetings—repairing boats, exchanging spouses, performing deer rites—then dispersed again into estuaries.

Key sites: Star Carr (Vale of Pickering); Howick and coastal North Sea Mesolithic camps; Irish Mesolithic coastal sites (e.g. Mount Sandel tradition); Oronsay and western Scottish shell middens.

Key people / anonymity: No named individuals; Star Carr’s frontleted performers remain anonymous.
britain.ancestryNote: ~Pure WHG before farming; later turnovers remove most of this lineage.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown. Not Celtic — Insular Celtic is an Iron Age/historical stage.
britain.summary: Post-Doggerland island WHG foragers of Britain and Ireland—wetland platforms, microliths, and low-density coastal rounds before farming’s near-total replacement.

france.culture:
Small flexible bands; social capital was knowledge of flint and game. Brittany’s Atlantic façade and Languedoc’s Mediterranean edge developed craft dialects within one forager world. Burials with ochre and curated goods imply respect for persons without recoverable chiefly titles.

Meeting places at fords and flint sources likely doubled as marriage markets; Mesolithic ‘politics’ was the management of distance between kin camps.

Key sites: Tardenoisian type areas of the Paris Basin / Île-de-France; Sauveterrian southern French rock shelters; Atlantic Breton Mesolithic coastal sites; Riverscape camps of the Loire and Seine basins.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous forager bands; facies names are modern labels.
france.linguisticNote: Unattested; later Gaulish is Celtic IE and unrelated in any recoverable way.
france.ancestryNote: WHG-dominated; EEF arrives with Cardial/LBK streams later.
france.summary: Microlithic WHG foragers of post-glacial Gaul—forest and river economies from Brittany to Languedoc before dual Cardial and LBK farming streams.

central.culture:
Mobile bands; social ties through flint exchange and marriage. Rock art rarer than in Atlantic/Alpine zones; aesthetic energy in projectile geometry and ornament. Status, when visible, is burial care and amber, not residences.

Low archaeological ‘loudness’ should not be mistaken for social simplicity; amber and flint paths imply obligations stretching farther than a single valley’s hunt.

Key sites: Mesolithic camps of the North European Plain (Elbe–Rhine zone); Alpine foreland lakeside forager sites; Amber-bearing coastal contact finds; Flint procurement locales later reused by LBK.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested personal names.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown forager languages; not Germanic or Celtic.
central.ancestryNote: WHG-dominated core of the North European Plain; EHG affinity rises eastward toward the forest-steppe divide.
central.summary: WHG foragers of the North European Plain and Alpine foreland—forest-river economies on the soft western edge of the later EHG ‘great divide.’

scandinavia.culture:
Coastal and inland rounds; dugouts and leisters enable dense wetland living. Amber animals and beads mark prestige. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.

Seal rookeries and salmon runs create defendable, memorable places; northern politics begins with knowing which skerries feed which kin.

Key sites: Maglemose wetland sites of Zealand and southern Scandinavia; Kongemose culture coastal sites; Fosna–Hensbacka pioneer sites of Norway/west Sweden; Early Scandinavian amber find contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous seal-hunters and wetland dwellers.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Unknown. Pre-Germanic is associated with much later Battle Axe / Nordic BA stages.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: SHG = northern foragers often modeled as WHG + elevated EHG-related affinity; Maglemosian–Kongemose world.
scandinavia.summary: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers of wetlands and rising Baltic/North Sea shores—WHG with elevated EHG affinity—before TRB farming.

italy.culture:
Small bands; identity local to valley and coast. North–south and sea-to-sea contrasts in foraging strategies. Exchange of shell and early obsidian foreshadows network Italy.

Tyrrhenian versus Adriatic shores teach different winds and molluscs; Italian forager society is already a peninsula of specialised coasts linked by ridge paths. Small bands still meet at passes where Alpine and Apennine seasons reverse.

Key sites: Epigravettian–Mesolithic rock shelters of the Apennines and Alps; Coastal Mesolithic camps of Liguria and southern Italy; Early Lipari obsidian find contexts in forager assemblages; Adriatic versus Tyrrhenian coastal forager facies.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested names.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown. Historical Etruscan and Italic are not Mesolithic holdovers in any demonstrated sense.
italy.ancestryNote: WHG-related; distinctive southern diversity vs northern WHG.
italy.summary: Peninsula WHG foragers after the Late Glacial—coastal and mountain rounds, early obsidian awareness—before Impressa maritime farming.

balkans.culture:
Semi-sedentary riverside communities with house burials and curated ornaments of shell and stone. Social density exceeds typical northern bands. Contact skills matter as much as fishing skills.

House burials and sculptural investment imply longer residential commitment than northern microlith camps; Iron Gates society could stage denser ritual publics beside the catch. Ornaments of shell and stone mark persons who live by a corridor, not a refuge myth.

Key sites: Lepenski Vir; Padina, Vlasac, and related Iron Gates sites; Danube gorge terraces; Early contact horizons with Starčevo farmers.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous sculptors and house-builders of Lepenski Vir; no historical names.
balkans.ancestryNote: Iron Gates HG ≠ generic western WHG; models treat them as a separate source/proxy.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown. Not Greek, Thracian, or Slavic — all far later.
balkans.summary: Danube Iron Gates foragers—trapezoidal houses, fish-human sculpture, distinctive HG genetics—contact corridor before Anatolian-related farming.

eastern.culture:
Hunter-fisher identity with ceramics optional. Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning. Wide-ranging lithic procurement and waterway travel structure alliance more than villages.

Rich graves imply that even low-density foragers could sustain hereditary or achieved rank loud enough to dress the dead for an audience of the living. Waterway travel and wide lithic catches structure alliance more than villages do.

Key sites: Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov cemetery; Volga–Oka and related forest forager sites; Pontic steppe-edge Mesolithic camps; Eastern forager ceramic (pre-farming) contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous ranked burial persons; no historical names.
eastern.ancestryNote: EHG-dominated forest-steppe; not WHG. Later a key source for WSH/Yamnaya with CHG-related ancestry.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown. Proto-Indo-European is reconstructed for a much later steppe horizon.
eastern.summary: EHG forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity—amber-rich burials, optional pottery, not yet Yamnaya or Indo-European.

periods.linguistics: Speech is entirely unattested. Later farmer and Indo-European languages are not continuous with recoverable Mesolithic tongues. Treat all language labels here as placeholders for lost diversity.

mapLayers.label: Azilian
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Azilian: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this dominant layer on the Mesolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Azilian ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Azilian. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Azilian: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

ESP.name: Iberian Mesolithic bands
ESP.summary: Post-glacial WHG foragers of Atlantic and Mediterranean Iberia, living by seasonal rounds of shellfish, deer, and upland game before Cardial farming.
ESP.conflicts: Local territorial foraging ranges; no states. Later replaced demographically by Cardial farmers.
ESP.religion: Belief systems unrecoverable in detail. Ritual archaeology: ochre-stained and curated burials, rare structured deposits, and landscape reuse of Paleolithic art places.
ESP.culture:
Society organised around mobile kinship bands rather than villages. Labour divided by age and season: coastal shellfish weeks, inland hunting stands, and curated visits to caves that still held Paleolithic images as remembered places. Personal ornaments—shell beads, ochre-stained bone—signalled affiliation more loudly than architecture. Conflict left few mass graves; violence, when present, was likely interpersonal or raid-scale.

Exchange was local-to-regional: good flint, marine shell inland, and shared projectile geometries. There were no chiefs recoverable by title; status, if ranked at all, shows in burial care and exotic beads rather than residences.

Key sites: El Mazo (Asturias shell midden sequences); Cantabrian Azilian rock shelters; Portuguese Atlantic Mesolithic middens (Tagus/Sado); Levantine Geometric Mesolithic sites.

Key people / anonymity: No historically named individuals. Social memory survives only as anonymous burial persons and site excavators’ type names.

GBR.name: British Mesolithic foragers
GBR.summary: Post-Doggerland island WHG foragers of Britain and Ireland—wetland platforms, microliths, and low-density coastal rounds before farming’s near-total replacement.
GBR.conflicts: Competition for coastal/river resources among small bands; later erased genetically by farmers then Beaker migrants.
GBR.religion: No recoverable pantheon. Shell-midden and cave burials, ochre, and curated human bone suggest ancestor/body rites; cosmology itself stays opaque.
GBR.culture:
Bands managed seasonal rounds from upland hunting to estuary fishing. Timber platforms and rare ritual gear (red-deer frontlets) suggest episodic aggregation and performance beside wetlands. Ireland and Britain shared canoe-and-trap aesthetics more than carved monuments.

Social scale remained small; exotic amber or shale beads mark occasional long links without chiefdom bureaucracy.

Wetland aggregation sites hint that even low-density islands staged periodic meetings—repairing boats, exchanging spouses, performing deer rites—then dispersed again into estuaries.

Key sites: Star Carr (Vale of Pickering); Howick and coastal North Sea Mesolithic camps; Irish Mesolithic coastal sites (e.g. Mount Sandel tradition); Oronsay and western Scottish shell middens.

Key people / anonymity: No named individuals; Star Carr’s frontleted performers remain anonymous.

FRA.name: Sauveterrian / Tardenoisian groups
FRA.summary: Microlithic WHG foragers of post-glacial Gaul—forest and river economies from Brittany to Languedoc before dual Cardial and LBK farming streams.
FRA.religion: Forager ritual poorly named. Archaeology shows careful burials, ochre, and occasional animal deposits — practice without readable myths.
FRA.culture:
Small flexible bands; social capital was knowledge of flint and game. Brittany’s Atlantic façade and Languedoc’s Mediterranean edge developed craft dialects within one forager world. Burials with ochre and curated goods imply respect for persons without recoverable chiefly titles.

Meeting places at fords and flint sources likely doubled as marriage markets; Mesolithic ‘politics’ was the management of distance between kin camps.

Key sites: Tardenoisian type areas of the Paris Basin / Île-de-France; Sauveterrian southern French rock shelters; Atlantic Breton Mesolithic coastal sites; Riverscape camps of the Loire and Seine basins.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous forager bands; facies names are modern labels.

DEU.name: Central European Mesolithic
DEU.summary: WHG foragers of the North European Plain and Alpine foreland—forest-river economies on the soft western edge of the later EHG ‘great divide.’
DEU.conflicts: No polities; later LBK farmers expand into these landscapes.
DEU.religion: Mesolithic belief content is lost. Scattered burials and structured faunal deposits hint at rites around death and animals, not temples or texts.
DEU.culture:
Mobile bands; social ties through flint exchange and marriage. Rock art rarer than in Atlantic/Alpine zones; aesthetic energy in projectile geometry and ornament. Status, when visible, is burial care and amber, not residences.

Low archaeological ‘loudness’ should not be mistaken for social simplicity; amber and flint paths imply obligations stretching farther than a single valley’s hunt.

Key sites: Mesolithic camps of the North European Plain (Elbe–Rhine zone); Alpine foreland lakeside forager sites; Amber-bearing coastal contact finds; Flint procurement locales later reused by LBK.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested personal names.

DNK.name: Maglemosian / Kongemose
DNK.summary: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers of wetlands and rising Baltic/North Sea shores—WHG with elevated EHG affinity—before TRB farming.
DNK.religion: Maglemosian–Kongemose ritual known mainly from graves and bog finds. No named gods; body treatment and wetland deposition are the evidence.
DNK.culture:
Coastal and inland rounds; dugouts and leisters enable dense wetland living. Amber animals and beads mark prestige. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.

Seal rookeries and salmon runs create defendable, memorable places; northern politics begins with knowing which skerries feed which kin.

Key sites: Maglemose wetland sites of Zealand and southern Scandinavia; Kongemose culture coastal sites; Fosna–Hensbacka pioneer sites of Norway/west Sweden; Early Scandinavian amber find contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous seal-hunters and wetland dwellers.

ITA.name: Epigravettian-descended foragers
ITA.summary: Peninsula WHG foragers after the Late Glacial—coastal and mountain rounds, early obsidian awareness—before Impressa maritime farming.
ITA.conflicts: Southern refugia matter for later WHG diversity.
ITA.religion: Epigravettian-descended foragers leave burial and ornament evidence; Mediterranean rock shelters hold ritual deposits without readable theology.
ITA.culture:
Small bands; identity local to valley and coast. North–south and sea-to-sea contrasts in foraging strategies. Exchange of shell and early obsidian foreshadows network Italy.

Tyrrhenian versus Adriatic shores teach different winds and molluscs; Italian forager society is already a peninsula of specialised coasts linked by ridge paths. Small bands still meet at passes where Alpine and Apennine seasons reverse.

Key sites: Epigravettian–Mesolithic rock shelters of the Apennines and Alps; Coastal Mesolithic camps of Liguria and southern Italy; Early Lipari obsidian find contexts in forager assemblages; Adriatic versus Tyrrhenian coastal forager facies.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested names.

SRB.name: Iron Gates foragers
SRB.summary: Danube Iron Gates foragers—trapezoidal houses, fish-human sculpture, distinctive HG genetics—contact corridor before Anatolian-related farming.
SRB.conflicts: Distinctive local identity before Starčevo farmers; contact and absorption follow.
SRB.religion: Iron Gates cemeteries show elaborate body treatment, sculptures, and house–burial links — unusually rich ritual archaeology for Mesolithic Europe.
SRB.culture:
Semi-sedentary riverside communities with house burials and curated ornaments of shell and stone. Social density exceeds typical northern bands. Contact skills matter as much as fishing skills.

House burials and sculptural investment imply longer residential commitment than northern microlith camps; Iron Gates society could stage denser ritual publics beside the catch. Ornaments of shell and stone mark persons who live by a corridor, not a refuge myth.

Key sites: Lepenski Vir; Padina, Vlasac, and related Iron Gates sites; Danube gorge terraces; Early contact horizons with Starčevo farmers.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous sculptors and house-builders of Lepenski Vir; no historical names.

UKR.name: Ukrainian Mesolithic
UKR.summary: EHG forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity—amber-rich burials, optional pottery, not yet Yamnaya or Indo-European.
UKR.conflicts: East of later Neolithic “great divide”; EHG-related.
UKR.religion: Forest-steppe forager ritual: burials with ochre and grave goods. Named gods and afterlife doctrines are not recoverable.
UKR.culture:
Hunter-fisher identity with ceramics optional. Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning. Wide-ranging lithic procurement and waterway travel structure alliance more than villages.

Rich graves imply that even low-density foragers could sustain hereditary or achieved rank loud enough to dress the dead for an audience of the living. Waterway travel and wide lithic catches structure alliance more than villages do.

Key sites: Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov cemetery; Volga–Oka and related forest forager sites; Pontic steppe-edge Mesolithic camps; Eastern forager ceramic (pre-farming) contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous ranked burial persons; no historical names.

PRT.summary: Post-glacial WHG foragers of Atlantic and Mediterranean Iberia, living by seasonal rounds of shellfish, deer, and upland game before Cardial farming.
PRT.culture:
Society organised around mobile kinship bands rather than villages. Labour divided by age and season: coastal shellfish weeks, inland hunting stands, and curated visits to caves that still held Paleolithic images as remembered places. Personal ornaments—shell beads, ochre-stained bone—signalled affiliation more loudly than architecture. Conflict left few mass graves; violence, when present, was likely interpersonal or raid-scale.

Exchange was local-to-regional: good flint, marine shell inland, and shared projectile geometries. There were no chiefs recoverable by title; status, if ranked at all, shows in burial care and exotic beads rather than residences.

Key sites: El Mazo (Asturias shell midden sequences); Cantabrian Azilian rock shelters; Portuguese Atlantic Mesolithic middens (Tagus/Sado); Levantine Geometric Mesolithic sites.

Key people / anonymity: No historically named individuals. Social memory survives only as anonymous burial persons and site excavators’ type names.

IRL.summary: Post-Doggerland island WHG foragers of Britain and Ireland—wetland platforms, microliths, and low-density coastal rounds before farming’s near-total replacement.
IRL.culture:
Bands managed seasonal rounds from upland hunting to estuary fishing. Timber platforms and rare ritual gear (red-deer frontlets) suggest episodic aggregation and performance beside wetlands. Ireland and Britain shared canoe-and-trap aesthetics more than carved monuments.

Social scale remained small; exotic amber or shale beads mark occasional long links without chiefdom bureaucracy.

Wetland aggregation sites hint that even low-density islands staged periodic meetings—repairing boats, exchanging spouses, performing deer rites—then dispersed again into estuaries.

Key sites: Star Carr (Vale of Pickering); Howick and coastal North Sea Mesolithic camps; Irish Mesolithic coastal sites (e.g. Mount Sandel tradition); Oronsay and western Scottish shell middens.

Key people / anonymity: No named individuals; Star Carr’s frontleted performers remain anonymous.

MCO.summary: Microlithic WHG foragers of post-glacial Gaul—forest and river economies from Brittany to Languedoc before dual Cardial and LBK farming streams.
MCO.culture:
Small flexible bands; social capital was knowledge of flint and game. Brittany’s Atlantic façade and Languedoc’s Mediterranean edge developed craft dialects within one forager world. Burials with ochre and curated goods imply respect for persons without recoverable chiefly titles.

Meeting places at fords and flint sources likely doubled as marriage markets; Mesolithic ‘politics’ was the management of distance between kin camps.

Key sites: Tardenoisian type areas of the Paris Basin / Île-de-France; Sauveterrian southern French rock shelters; Atlantic Breton Mesolithic coastal sites; Riverscape camps of the Loire and Seine basins.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous forager bands; facies names are modern labels.

POL.summary: WHG foragers of the North European Plain and Alpine foreland—forest-river economies on the soft western edge of the later EHG ‘great divide.’
POL.culture:
Mobile bands; social ties through flint exchange and marriage. Rock art rarer than in Atlantic/Alpine zones; aesthetic energy in projectile geometry and ornament. Status, when visible, is burial care and amber, not residences.

Low archaeological ‘loudness’ should not be mistaken for social simplicity; amber and flint paths imply obligations stretching farther than a single valley’s hunt.

Key sites: Mesolithic camps of the North European Plain (Elbe–Rhine zone); Alpine foreland lakeside forager sites; Amber-bearing coastal contact finds; Flint procurement locales later reused by LBK.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous; no attested personal names.

FIN.summary: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers of wetlands and rising Baltic/North Sea shores—WHG with elevated EHG affinity—before TRB farming.
FIN.culture:
Coastal and inland rounds; dugouts and leisters enable dense wetland living. Amber animals and beads mark prestige. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.

Seal rookeries and salmon runs create defendable, memorable places; northern politics begins with knowing which skerries feed which kin.

Key sites: Maglemose wetland sites of Zealand and southern Scandinavia; Kongemose culture coastal sites; Fosna–Hensbacka pioneer sites of Norway/west Sweden; Early Scandinavian amber find contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous seal-hunters and wetland dwellers.

Hunter-fisher identity with ceramics optional. Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning. Wide-ranging lithic procurement and waterway travel structure alliance more than villages.

Rich graves imply that even low-density foragers could sustain hereditary or achieved rank loud enough to dress the dead for an audience of the living. Waterway travel and wide lithic catches structure alliance more than villages do.

Key sites: Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov cemetery; Volga–Oka and related forest forager sites; Pontic steppe-edge Mesolithic camps; Eastern forager ceramic (pre-farming) contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous ranked burial persons; no historical names.

periods.label: First farmers on two corridors
periods.narrative: By the mid-sixth millennium BC Anatolian-related farmers push into Europe by sea (Cardial/Impresso) and up the Danube (Starčevo–LBK). Early farmer genomes are strongly EEF; local hunter-gatherers persist as Ertebølle holdouts in the north and Narva–Comb Ware farther east. This is demic farming spread, not a pan-European ethnic conversion — and still centuries before steppe ancestry.
periods.culturesNote: Cardial, Impresso, LBK, Starčevo–Vinča + HG holdouts (Ertebølle, Narva/Comb Ware, EHG persistence).

iberia.culture:
Household and herd replaced band and seasonal round as the basic social unit. Labour focused on clearing, sowing, milking, and potting; kinship likely organised land clearance and livestock inheritance even without written law. Pioneer settlements hugged coasts and river mouths where maritime logistics and Mediterranean crops worked best.

Identity advertised itself on ceramic surfaces—shell-stamped pots as badges of belonging. Interaction with foragers ranged from exchange and intermarriage (minor early) to spatial segregation; genomes show replacement first, admixture later.

Key sites: Early Cardial sites of Catalonia and Valencia; Andalusian Early Neolithic coastal settlements; Portuguese Estremadura Early Neolithic; Cova de l’Or / related impressed-ware caves (regional exemplars).

Key people / anonymity: No named historical persons. ‘Cardial’ is an archaeological ware label, not a polity or prophet.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early Iberian farmers ≈ 85–95% EEF in published models; WHG minority.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE farmer language(s). Not ancestral Basque or Iberian by evidence — those are later attestations.
iberia.summary: Seafaring Anatolian-related farmers bring cereals, sheep, and shell-stamped pottery along Iberia’s Mediterranean and Atlantic littoral, largely replacing WHG ancestry.

britain.culture:
Fixed houses, herds, and cereal stores reorganised kinship around land and livestock. Timber halls and early monuments imply communal labour and feasting politics. Enclosures gathered people for rites and negotiation—soft regional institutions without kings we can name.

Timber halls and interrupted-ditch enclosures concentrate labour debts and feast obligations; Neolithic society learns to schedule people as carefully as seed.

Key sites: Early Neolithic houses and halls (e.g. Irish rectangular house horizons); Southern British causewayed enclosures (Windmill Hill tradition); Early long barrows of Wessex and the Cotswolds; Carinated Bowl pottery assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous pioneer farmers; no attested leaders.
britain.ancestryNote: Earliest farming Britain: EEF-led; WHG higher at Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE. The later Celtic languages are not this Neolithic speech.

ancestryCline.label: Core pioneer → Atlantic edge
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher where farmers meet residual foragers; EEF highest in early pioneer packages.

britain.summary: Continental-derived farming reaches Britain and Ireland with strongly EEF genomes—the first major replacement of insular WHG—before later megalith florescence.

france.culture:
Two ceramic-and-house traditions meant two social dialects of farming meeting in Gaul. Household and enclosure began to replace pure seasonal round. Burial rites diverged—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin.

Where Cardial and LBK spheres approach, households may have recognised strangers by pot and house form before by speech—material dialect as social sorting.

Key sites: Mediterranean Cardial sites of Provence/Languedoc; LBK-related settlements of Alsace / Paris Basin northeast; Early Alpine jadeitite axe findspots in Gaul; Loess-terrace Early Neolithic villages.

Key people / anonymity: No named persons; ‘Cardial’ and ‘LBK’ are archaeological packages.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown farmer languages; Gaulish Celtic is ~4000+ years later.
france.ancestryNote: Early farmers ~EEF; WHG admixture increases through Middle Neolithic.
france.summary: France as hinge: Mediterranean Cardial along the littoral and Danubian LBK influence in the northeast—two EEF streams replacing most WHG.

central.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.
central.ancestryNote: Early LBK cores often >85% EEF; WHG rises later in Mid–Late Neolithic.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown; widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.

ancestryCline.label: LBK core → northern contact
ancestryCline.note: WHG higher toward northern/forest contact; EEF highest in loess LBK heartland.

central.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.

scandinavia.culture:
Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine mammal hunting and oyster seasons structure prestige and diet. Contact with LBK/TRB south is wary and porous.

Ertebølle communities can adopt pots and still refuse villages; identity is chosen package by package at the farmer contact zone. Shell middens remain the public monuments of a people who will not yet surrender the sea.

Key sites: Ertebølle and Bjørnsholm-type shell middens; Danish straits coastal forager settlements; Earliest TRB farming footholds in southern Scandinavia; Pointed-base pottery type assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous Ertebølle fishers and earliest TRB pioneers.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Ertebølle holdout still strong; earliest TRB farmers only beginning the first Holocene turnover.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Language shift likely with farming; details unknowable. Not Old Norse.

ancestryCline.label: Forager coast → earliest TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: SHG/WHG dominate Ertebølle coasts; EEF rises where earliest Funnelbeaker farming sticks.

scandinavia.summary: Ertebølle coastal foragers keep SHG ways and invent northern pottery while earliest Funnelbeaker farming only begins the first Holocene turnover.

italy.culture:
Villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Household shrines and figurines locate the sacred in domestic space. Obsidian specialists and sailors stitch islands to coasts.

Sailors, potters, and herders form the Early Neolithic public; mountain foragers remain neighbours whose knowledge of passes still matters to anyone moving flocks. Household burials and figurines locate belonging inside the settlement rather than the seasonal camp.

Key sites: Impressed Ware coastal settlements of Apulia and Sicily; Tyrrhenian Early Neolithic villages; Lipari and related obsidian workshops; Adriatic Impressa sites facing the Balkan shore.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous maritime pioneers and obsidian knappers.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown Impresso-related farmer speech — not Latin, not Etruscan, and not recoverable from later Italic.
italy.ancestryNote: Early Italian Impresso farmers are EEF-dominated in published models; WHG is a minority that rises later.
italy.summary: Maritime Impressed Ware farming along Italian coasts—EEF demic replacement and launch corridor toward France and Iberia.

balkans.culture:
Tell living stacks generations—the past literally underfoot. Household cults centre figurines; ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal. Craft and farming specialisation grow with settlement scale.

Tell neighbours stack obligations vertically: rebuilding on ancestors’ rubble is both practical and moral continuity. Figurine-rich households make ritual labour a daily chore, not a rare pilgrimage.

Key sites: Starčevo type sites; Körös and Criș settlement zones of the Carpathian Basin edge; Early Vinča tell settlements; Iron Gates contact-period mixed horizons.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tell villagers and figurine makers.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related languages. Ancient Greek is still far in the future and unrelated by attestation.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF majority + elevated local HG vs early LBK extremes.
balkans.summary: Europe’s first farming corridor—Anatolian-related tell villages, figurines, and elevated local HG admixture versus some western LBK extremes.

eastern.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya: EHG + CHG-related kept separate (not yet fused as WSH). Farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown mix; not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.

ancestryCline.label: Forest-steppe HG → farmer fringe
ancestryCline.note: EHG (+ some CHG-related) east of the Neolithic divide; EEF rises on Bug–Dniester contact — not WSH yet.

eastern.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.

periods.linguistics: No texts. Farmer languages are unknown and usually modeled as non-Indo-European. Residual forager languages vanish or leave only undetectable substrates. Do not equate “Neolithic” with any historically named family.

mapLayers.label: Cardial Ware
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Cardial Ware: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this incoming layer on the Early Neolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Cardial Ware ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Cardial Ware. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Cardial Ware: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

DEU.name: LBK pioneer villages
DEU.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.
DEU.conflicts: Expansion into forager landscapes; limited early conflict archaeologically visible as pioneer frontier.
DEU.religion: LBK farmers practiced domestic and enclosure ritual: foundation deposits, cattle offerings, and cemetery rows. Ancestor care and fertility rites are inferred; named gods are not.
DEU.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.

GBR.name: Earliest Neolithic arrival
GBR.summary: Continental-derived farming reaches Britain and Ireland with strongly EEF genomes—the first major replacement of insular WHG—before later megalith florescence.
GBR.conflicts: First major replacement of Mesolithic WHG.
GBR.religion: Earliest Neolithic Britain imports chambered-tomb and causewayed-enclosure rites: collective burial, feasting debris, and seasonal gathering places.
GBR.culture:
Fixed houses, herds, and cereal stores reorganised kinship around land and livestock. Timber halls and early monuments imply communal labour and feasting politics. Enclosures gathered people for rites and negotiation—soft regional institutions without kings we can name.

Timber halls and interrupted-ditch enclosures concentrate labour debts and feast obligations; Neolithic society learns to schedule people as carefully as seed.

Key sites: Early Neolithic houses and halls (e.g. Irish rectangular house horizons); Southern British causewayed enclosures (Windmill Hill tradition); Early long barrows of Wessex and the Cotswolds; Carinated Bowl pottery assemblages.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous pioneer farmers; no attested leaders.

UKR.name: Bug–Dniester / farmer fringe
UKR.summary: East of the Neolithic genomic divide: EHG foragers and Comb Ware aesthetics meet only a western Cucuteni–Trypillia farmer fringe—not pan-eastern EEF replacement.
UKR.religion: Bug–Dniester / farmer-fringe ritual mixes forager burial habits with incoming agrarian figurines and domestic deposits along the contact zone.
UKR.culture:
Plural frontier: forager burial richness continues; farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics at the contact fringe. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are logistics backbone.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.

PRT.summary: Seafaring Anatolian-related farmers bring cereals, sheep, and shell-stamped pottery along Iberia’s Mediterranean and Atlantic littoral, largely replacing WHG ancestry.
PRT.culture:
Household and herd replaced band and seasonal round as the basic social unit. Labour focused on clearing, sowing, milking, and potting; kinship likely organised land clearance and livestock inheritance even without written law. Pioneer settlements hugged coasts and river mouths where maritime logistics and Mediterranean crops worked best.

Identity advertised itself on ceramic surfaces—shell-stamped pots as badges of belonging. Interaction with foragers ranged from exchange and intermarriage (minor early) to spatial segregation; genomes show replacement first, admixture later.

Key sites: Early Cardial sites of Catalonia and Valencia; Andalusian Early Neolithic coastal settlements; Portuguese Estremadura Early Neolithic; Cova de l’Or / related impressed-ware caves (regional exemplars).

Key people / anonymity: No named historical persons. ‘Cardial’ is an archaeological ware label, not a polity or prophet.

FRA.summary: France as hinge: Mediterranean Cardial along the littoral and Danubian LBK influence in the northeast—two EEF streams replacing most WHG.
FRA.culture:
Two ceramic-and-house traditions meant two social dialects of farming meeting in Gaul. Household and enclosure began to replace pure seasonal round. Burial rites diverged—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin.

Where Cardial and LBK spheres approach, households may have recognised strangers by pot and house form before by speech—material dialect as social sorting.

Key sites: Mediterranean Cardial sites of Provence/Languedoc; LBK-related settlements of Alsace / Paris Basin northeast; Early Alpine jadeitite axe findspots in Gaul; Loess-terrace Early Neolithic villages.

Key people / anonymity: No named persons; ‘Cardial’ and ‘LBK’ are archaeological packages.

POL.summary: Classic Central European Early Neolithic: longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, loess pioneer farming—strongly EEF, not Celtic or Germanic.
POL.culture:
Longhouse villages invent agrarian social architecture: aDNA often supports patrilocal kinship, cattle wealth, and rapid fission-colonisation. Cemeteries stage gendered tool kits. Crisis centuries reveal massacre and ritualised processing of bodies as dark limits of community.

Patrilocal signals in aDNA, if read cautiously, align with longhouse politics where in-marrying women joined cattle-rich timber lineages—and where late massacres show how brittle that order could become.

Key sites: Bylany and classic Bohemian/Moravian LBK settlements; Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten massacre sites; Herxheim ritual enclosure; Loess-belt longhouse villages of the Rhine–Danube corridors.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous villagers and victims of late LBK massacres; no royal names.

SMR.summary: Maritime Impressed Ware farming along Italian coasts—EEF demic replacement and launch corridor toward France and Iberia.
SMR.culture:
Villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Household shrines and figurines locate the sacred in domestic space. Obsidian specialists and sailors stitch islands to coasts.

Sailors, potters, and herders form the Early Neolithic public; mountain foragers remain neighbours whose knowledge of passes still matters to anyone moving flocks. Household burials and figurines locate belonging inside the settlement rather than the seasonal camp.

Key sites: Impressed Ware coastal settlements of Apulia and Sicily; Tyrrhenian Early Neolithic villages; Lipari and related obsidian workshops; Adriatic Impressa sites facing the Balkan shore.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous maritime pioneers and obsidian knappers.

BGR.summary: Europe’s first farming corridor—Anatolian-related tell villages, figurines, and elevated local HG admixture versus some western LBK extremes.
BGR.culture:
Tell living stacks generations—the past literally underfoot. Household cults centre figurines; ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal. Craft and farming specialisation grow with settlement scale.

Tell neighbours stack obligations vertically: rebuilding on ancestors’ rubble is both practical and moral continuity. Figurine-rich households make ritual labour a daily chore, not a rare pilgrimage.

Key sites: Starčevo type sites; Körös and Criș settlement zones of the Carpathian Basin edge; Early Vinča tell settlements; Iron Gates contact-period mixed horizons.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tell villagers and figurine makers.

Frontier etiquette—gift, raid, marriage, avoidance—matters more than any single ‘Neolithic conversion’ sermon along the Dniester–Bug line. Forager burial richness and farmer fringe figurines can coexist for centuries.

Key sites: Comb Ware forest zone sites; Precucuteni / early Trypillia fringe settlements; Dniester–Bug river corridor contact sites; Pontic steppe forager camps contemporary with farmer fringe.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous frontier foragers and fringe farmers.

periods.label: Megaliths densify farmer Europe
periods.narrative: Near 3800 BC farmer societies thicken: Atlantic passage graves, Chasséen and Michelsberg inland, Funnelbeaker (TRB) across the north European plain, Cucuteni–Trypillia mega-settlements on the east. WHG ancestry has climbed inside many farmer groups — higher on Atlantic and northern façades — while Pitted Ware and Narva foragers still fringe the coasts. Steppe pastoralists have not yet remade the temperate gene pool.
periods.culturesNote: TRB, Michelsberg, Chasséen, megalithic Atlantic, GAC, Trypillia + HG holdouts (Pitted Ware, Narva/Comb Ware).

iberia.culture:
Collective burial and tomb re-entry invent a politics of ancestry: who belongs is argued in chambers and offerings. Labour for quarrying and levering stones implies seasonal aggregation beyond the single household. Prestige goods mark differentiation short of named kings.

Villages and herding intensified on Atlantic and southern soils; monument clusters suggest regional pilgrimage and alliance without a single Iberian capital.

Tomb re-entry across generations turns kinship into a public archive: bones are rearranged, offerings refreshed, and claims on pasture rehearsed in front of the dead.

Key sites: Antequera dolmens (Menga, Viera, El Romeral); Atlantic Portuguese and Galician passage graves; Alentejo / southwestern engraved schist plaque zones; Los Millares precursor landscapes (toward Copper Age).

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous tomb builders and plaque carvers; no attested rulers or sages.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Historical Iberian script languages are Copper/Iron Age attestations, not proven megalithic speech.
iberia.ancestryNote: EEF majority; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic façades than in southern inland cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic façade → inland south
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises toward Atlantic megalithic zones; EEF higher inland/south.

iberia.summary: Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved plaques turn Atlantic and southern Iberia into ancestor theatres while EEF farmers absorb renewed WHG ancestry—still pre-steppe.

britain.culture:
Monument clusters imply regional gathering, labour mobilisation, and competitive prestige among farming communities. Kinship and land claims were argued in stone: who builds, who buries, who feasts. Specialised flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show craft economies feeding ritual and clearance alike.

Quarry crews, tomb teams, and feast hosts form overlapping labour publics; prestige accrues to those who can move stone and meat at landscape scale.

Key sites: Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth); Maeshowe and Orkney World Heritage monuments; Skara Brae; Stonehenge landscape (pre-/early stone phases in this era’s long tail); Langdale axe quarries; Grimes Graves flint mines.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous astronomer-builders and quarry specialists; no attested personal names.
britain.ancestryNote: Neolithic Britain without steppe; WHG higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE; later Celtic is not continuous by default.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → southern farming
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher in northern/western Neolithic landscapes; EEF higher in denser southern farming.

britain.summary: Boyne Valley, Orkney, and Wessex monument societies—EEF+WHG farmers whose stone cosmologies precede Beaker demographic collapse.

france.culture:
Chasséen networks standardised pottery and flint across wide tracts—a soft political grammar. Monument labour on Armorica implies seasonal aggregation and prestige competition. Enclosures gathered people for feasts and boundary-making inland.

Alignment and tumulus projects imply sponsors able to call labour across multiple settlements—soft hierarchies visible in stone even without named lords.

Key sites: Carnac alignments (Ménec, Kermario); Tumulus Saint-Michel / Morbihan monumental tombs; Cairn of Barnenez; Chasséen enclosure and settlement sites of interior France.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous alignment builders and jade-axe patrons; no attested names.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-Celtic farmer languages of Chasséen/megalithic France; Gaulish appears only in the Iron Age record.
france.ancestryNote: EEF majority + WHG; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic west than in eastern Chasséen cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic west → eastern Chasséen
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher on the megalithic Atlantic façade; EEF higher in eastern Chasséen farming.

france.summary: Carnac alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Chasséen networks—Atlantic ritual economies and interior enclosures in a still pre-steppe EEF+WHG France.

central.culture:
Enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary earthworks as political technology. Flint daggers and specialist mining (Rijckholt tradition) mark status and industry. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

Enclosure feasts redistribute meat and obligations; Middle Neolithic politics is calendrical as much as territorial.

Key sites: Michelsberg enclosure sites of the Rhineland; Northern TRB megalithic tombs (North European Plain); Rijckholt and related flint-mine systems; Early Globular Amphora burial contexts.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous enclosure builders and flint miners.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown. CW-linked IE comes next, not yet.
central.ancestryNote: TRB/Michelsberg farmers: WHG higher in northern TRB; EEF higher in southern/central agricultural cores. GAC forms as the farmer side later mixed into Corded Ware.

ancestryCline.label: Northern TRB → central/south core
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises north (and toward forager contact); EEF highest in Michelsberg / southern TRB cores.

central.summary: Post-LBK regionalisation: Michelsberg enclosures, Funnelbeaker north, rising WHG in farmers, early GAC—still pre-steppe.

scandinavia.culture:
Tomb building and forest clearance mobilise communal labour. Dual TRB/Pitted Ware lifeways mean parallel prestige systems—cattle and flint inland, seals and marine hunting on coasts. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige.

TRB tomb builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters may share beaches and still refuse each other’s full moral economy—parallel Scandinavias in one era. Cattle feasts and seal oil lamps light different nights of the same archipelago.

Key sites: Danish TRB dolmens and passage graves; Early Scandinavian flint mines; Pitted Ware coastal sites (e.g. Ajvide-type contexts in wider tradition); Southern Swedish TRB farming settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous dolmen builders and Pitted Ware seal hunters.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Unknown TRB-related speech; pre-Germanic tied to later Battle Axe models.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: TRB farmers inland/south vs Pitted Ware forager holdouts on coasts — two genetic regimes under one map period.

ancestryCline.label: Pitted Ware coasts → TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: Coastal Pitted Ware keeps high SHG/WHG; southern/inland TRB is EEF-led with residual HG.

scandinavia.summary: TRB farmers bring cereals, cattle, and dolmens north while Pitted Ware coastal foragers keep SHG-rich seal hunting—two genetic regimes under one map period.

italy.culture:
Regional pottery fashions mark identities across a still-EEF genetic world with rising local HG admixture. Craft specialisation and exotic stone mark status gradients without palaces.

Grave goods begin to sort persons more loudly; Italy’s Middle Neolithic learns ranking without yet inventing palace redistributive states. Obsidian and greenstone specialists stitch coasts to Alpine paths.

Key sites: Serra d’Alto and Diana culture type sites; Obsidian-rich Middle Neolithic settlements; Alpine foreland early copper contexts (toward Remedello); Statue-menhir and megalithic zones of Alpine/Italian regions.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous potters, sailors, and early metal experimenters.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown; pre-Italic / pre-Etruscan deep layers unrecoverable.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF-led; steppe arrives mainly in the Bronze Age.
italy.summary: Diana, Serra d’Alto, and related farmer cultures—fine wares, rising HG admixture, Alpine jade and island stone—copper glinting at the northern edge.

balkans.culture:
Tell mega-villages support craft specialists. House-based ritual and possible intentional house burning encode renewal cycles. Ranking visible in goods before palace economies.

Craft specialists on copper and fine ware imply patronage and surplus; ranking rises without dissolving household ritual centres into temple bureaucracy. Tell mega-villages concentrate people who still bury and burn close to home.

Key sites: Vinča-Belo Brdo and major Vinča tells; Pločnik and related early copper contexts; Late Neolithic tell belts of the middle Danube; Sites with Vinča symbols / notations.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous metallurgists and figurine makers; Vinča symbols have no deciphered authors.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown. Mycenaean Greek is still a millennium+ away.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF+local HG; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age.
balkans.summary: Dense tells, Vinča dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, early copper—proto-metal complexity with debated Vinča symbols, still mostly pre-steppe.

eastern.culture:
Low-hierarchy mega-population experiments—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle and manure management sustain aggregation. Neighboring steppe burial politics offer a contrasting social grammar just beyond the painted-pottery world.

Megasite circuits imply assembly rules—where houses face, how cattle are fenced, when houses burn—soft urbanism without kings. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic burial politics offer a contrasting grammar just beyond the painted rings.

Key sites: Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki megasites; Cucuteni painted-pottery heartlands; Usatove and Serednii Stih Eneolithic steppe contexts; Burned-house horizons of Trypillia settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous megasite planners and potters; steppe Eneolithic burial elites remain nameless.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya Pontic: EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF — forming steppe package, not scored as WSH yet.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown. Possible early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.

ancestryCline.label: Trypillia farms → Pontic steppe edge
ancestryCline.note: EEF higher in Trypillia; EHG/CHG-related rise toward Usatove / Serednii Stih (pre-WSH fusion).

eastern.summary: Trypillia megasites and swirling painted pottery meet Eneolithic steppe groups—pre-Yamnaya crucible of EEF, EHG, and CHG-related ancestries.

periods.linguistics: Still pre-Indo-European across most of Europe. Megalithic and Trypillia labels are not language families. Possible early IE on the steppe edge only as hypothesis.

mapLayers.label: Atlantic megalithic
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Atlantic megalithic: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this dominant layer on the Middle–Late Neolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Atlantic megalithic ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Atlantic megalithic. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Atlantic megalithic: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

GBR.name: British megalith builders
GBR.summary: Boyne Valley, Orkney, and Wessex monument societies—EEF+WHG farmers whose stone cosmologies precede Beaker demographic collapse.
GBR.conflicts: Regional monument competition; gene pool later collapses in Beaker age.
GBR.religion: Atlantic megalithic religion: collective tombs, ancestor bone circulation, and solar-aligned monuments (e.g. Stonehenge landscape). Ritual feasting at causewayed enclosures.

BLR.summary: Trypillia megasites and swirling painted pottery meet Eneolithic steppe groups—pre-Yamnaya crucible of EEF, EHG, and CHG-related ancestries.
BLR.culture:
Low-hierarchy mega-population experiments—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle and manure management sustain aggregation. Neighboring steppe burial politics offer a contrasting social grammar just beyond the painted-pottery world.

Megasite circuits imply assembly rules—where houses face, how cattle are fenced, when houses burn—soft urbanism without kings. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic burial politics offer a contrasting grammar just beyond the painted rings.

Key sites: Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki megasites; Cucuteni painted-pottery heartlands; Usatove and Serednii Stih Eneolithic steppe contexts; Burned-house horizons of Trypillia settlements.

Key people / anonymity: Anonymous megasite planners and potters; steppe Eneolithic burial elites remain nameless.

periods.label: Yamnaya on the steppe edge
periods.narrative: At 3000 BC Yamnaya wagon-and-herd societies dominate the Pontic–Caspian steppe while Late Neolithic farmer Europe — TRB, Globular Amphora, Iberian Copper Age, British monument builders — continues west. Steppe-related ancestry is high on the core steppe and falls off as a gradient, not an instant coat. Comparative linguistics places early Indo-European speech in this horizon; western Europe is not yet Corded or Beaker.
periods.culturesNote: Yamnaya/Yamna, Afanasievo (eastward), late Trypillia, Usatove contacts, Remedello/Gaudo in Italy, late TRB/Pitted Ware in the north.

iberia.culture: Copper Age Iberian society organises around fortified hilltop centres, craft specialisation, and collective tombs that imply corporate kinship rather than steppe pastoral kings. Households farm Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while workshops cast copper blades and shape schematic idols. Atlantic façades and the southeast speak related but not identical dialects of prestige—walls and tholoi in one zone, megalithic afterlives and coastal exchange in another. Belonging is local, ancestral, and increasingly unequal.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Do not equate Copper Age cultures with Celtic.
iberia.ancestryNote: Still largely EEF+WHG; steppe ≈ 0–few percent at Copper Age start.

britain.culture: Society gathers around henges, avenues, and seasonal monuments that structure time and labour. Households farm chalk and clay while investing surplus in timber and stone spectacles. Jet, amber, and stone ornaments mark persons inside a still-collective ceremonial order. Belonging is pilgrimage and monument rebuild, not single-grave martial kits.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE Neolithic speech about to be marginalized/replaced in IE-shift models.
britain.ancestryNote: Still Neolithic Britain — steppe negligible until Beaker.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → south
ancestryCline.note: Residual WHG cline within Late Neolithic Britain; steppe still ~0–few %.

france.culture: Collective tombs and regional ceramic traditions organise farmer communities even as new bloodlines enter northern families. Households keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems; prestige still speaks in polished axes and chamber access. Society is Neolithic in structure—ancestral corporations, megalithic rites—with pastoral signals rising in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.
france.ancestryNote: Site-variable early steppe (order ~10–20% in some modeled groups); not Britain-level replacement.
france.linguisticNote: Possible early IE speech with steppe gene flow — contested; no texts.
france.cultureLabel: Late Neolithic France — first steppe pulses

central.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.
central.linguisticNote: Leading archaeological correlate of early IE expansion into the European plain.
central.ancestryNote: Late TRB/GAC still farmer-led; early steppe signals uneven — higher toward the east.

ancestryCline.label: West GAC/TRB → eastern contact
ancestryCline.note: Steppe% rises east toward Pontic contact; western Late Neolithic stays more EEF+WHG.

scandinavia.culture: TRB farmsteads and megalithic chambers structure agrarian kinship; Pitted Ware camps organise sealing, fishing, and coastal exchange. Society is plural: pig and cattle ritual inland, marine mammal economies on the strand. Belonging is ecological as much as ethnic.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Pre-IE/transitional; pre-Germanic linked to ensuing Battle Axe/SGC.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Mostly pre–Single Grave; Pitted Ware coasts keep HG-rich profiles beside TRB farms.

ancestryCline.label: Pitted Ware → late TRB
ancestryCline.note: Coastal holdouts stay HG-rich; southern TRB is EEF-led with only slight early steppe.

italy.culture: Weapon-grave and chamber-tomb communities organise honour around metal kits and subterranean ancestry. Households farm Mediterranean crops; specialists cast copper. Alpine and peninsular provinces keep distinct burial dialects while sharing the Copper Age turn toward inequality and craft.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown. Historical Italic and Etruscan are still ahead.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF+WHG Copper Age Italy; no detectable steppe ancestry yet.

balkans.culture: Riverine farmers, tell communities, and incoming pastoral groups negotiate space along the Danube and Black Sea fringe. Metallurgy, figurines, and cemetery rites keep inland farmer identities while steppe kits appear at edges. Society is corridor diplomacy in material form.
balkans.linguisticNote: Contact zone; Greek ancestor speech not yet Mycenaean-attested.
balkans.ancestryNote: Variable steppe on EEF-rich bases; not uniform Yamnaya replacement.

eastern.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.
eastern.ancestryNote: Yamnaya = WSH package (EHG+CHG already fused). Shown as WSH, not re-split into EHG and CHG.
eastern.linguisticNote: Best archaeological match for late Proto-Indo-European (or a sister) in the steppe hypothesis — reconstructed lexicon, not Yamnaya inscriptions.

ancestryCline.label: Yamnaya core → farmer edge
ancestryCline.note: WSH% highest on Yamnaya core steppe; EEF rises toward late Trypillia / western contact.

periods.linguistics: Steppe speech is reconstructed only via Indo-European comparative method. Yamnaya ≈ late PIE (or a close sister) is mainstream but unprovable from inscriptions. Western Europe still largely non-IE.

mapLayers.label: Yamnaya core steppe
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Yamnaya core steppe: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this incoming layer on the Copper / Yamnaya map.
mapLayers.ideas: Yamnaya core steppe ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Yamnaya core steppe. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Yamnaya core steppe: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

UKR.name: Yamnaya pastoralists
UKR.summary: Kurgan steppe societies of the Pontic–Caspian zone.
UKR.conflicts: Expansion into Danube/Carpathian Basin; pressure on Trypillia and GAC worlds.
UKR.religion: Yamnaya steppe religion is read from kurgans: ochre-covered flexed burials, wagons/animal offerings, and stelae. Sky/ancestor pastoral cult inferred; no native texts.
UKR.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.

RUS.name: Yamnaya / steppe clans
RUS.conflicts: Formation zone of WSH ancestry; later Catacomb succeeds.
RUS.religion: Pontic–Caspian kurgan rite: single elite graves under mounds, ochre, weapons, and sacrificed animals — status afterlife and pastoral cosmology in earth and herd.
RUS.culture: Mobile pastoral households organise around herds, dairy, and kurgan lineages. Seasonal mobility and wagon transport structure life across the Pontic–Caspian. Society amplifies certain male lineages in later expansions; wealth is animals, milk stores, and grave theatre rather than urban surplus.

HUN.name: Yamnaya in the Carpathian Basin
HUN.conflicts: Contact/conflict with local Late Neolithic/Copper communities.
HUN.religion: Yamnaya-related Carpathian Basin graves import kurgan burial grammar (ochre, mounds, pastoral goods) into farmer Europe’s ritual map.
HUN.culture: Cattle-rich Globular Amphora households and late Funnelbeaker neighbours organise wealth around herds, amphorae, and flint. Eastern contact brings pastoral mobility and new burial politics without instantly erasing farmer settlements. Society stands between collective Neolithic claims and the single-grave order about to standardise gendered weapon kits across the plain.

ESP.name: Los Millares & Copper Age Iberia
ESP.conflicts: Internal hierarchy; Beaker package arrives before major steppe ancestry.
ESP.religion: Los Millares / Copper Age Iberia: fortified ritual centers, collective and emerging individual tombs, idol plaques — not Yamnaya kurgans, but parallel sacral intensification.
ESP.culture: Copper Age Iberian society organises around fortified hilltop centres, craft specialisation, and collective tombs that imply corporate kinship rather than steppe pastoral kings. Households farm Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while workshops cast copper blades and shape schematic idols. Atlantic façades and the southeast speak related but not identical dialects of prestige—walls and tholoi in one zone, megalithic afterlives and coastal exchange in another. Belonging is local, ancestral, and increasingly unequal.

GBR.name: Late Neolithic Britain
GBR.religion: Late Neolithic Britain: continuing megalithic and henge rites (Stonehenge landscape) before Beaker individual graves rewrite burial fashion.
GBR.culture: Society gathers around henges, avenues, and seasonal monuments that structure time and labour. Households farm chalk and clay while investing surplus in timber and stone spectacles. Jet, amber, and stone ornaments mark persons inside a still-collective ceremonial order. Belonging is pilgrimage and monument rebuild, not single-grave martial kits.

ITA.name: Remedello / Gaudo
ITA.conflicts: Limited early steppe vs CW north.
ITA.religion: Remedello / Gaudo: Copper Age cemeteries with weapon graves and formal rite — Italian paths to status burial without steppe kurgans.
ITA.culture: Weapon-grave and chamber-tomb communities organise honour around metal kits and subterranean ancestry. Households farm Mediterranean crops; specialists cast copper. Alpine and peninsular provinces keep distinct burial dialects while sharing the Copper Age turn toward inequality and craft.
